author: Rory Robinson
title: Bryson DeChambeau fears fellow players could stop him returning to PGA Tour - NewsBreak
text:
By Rory Robinson ,
1 hours ago Professional golf is moving toward unity, but Bryson DeChambeau believes tension among PGA Tour players could keep him from returning with LIV Golf's future still up in the air.
The former U.S. Open champion is already thinking about life after LIV Golf following reports that Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund could stop funding the league after the 2026 season. But he aimed a dig at the PGA Tour and hit out at potential punishments he could face.
While several LIV stars have stayed quiet publicly, DeChambeau has openly discussed everything from PGA Tour politics to growing his YouTube empire far beyond traditional golf television. He was also snubbed by Donald Trump as the President named his top three golfers.
• Rory McIlroy finally breaks silence on 'weird' controversy around Masters win
• Grant Horvat and suspended PGA Tour pro reveal full roster for new golf league
As LIV Golf prepares for this week’s tournament at Trump National Golf Club, DeChambeau admitted his path back to the PGA Tour may not depend on executives or commissioners at all. Instead, he feels that fellow players on tour could ultimately decide whether he feels welcome back to play.
"I think there’s a way to solve any problem," DeChambeau told Skratch Golf. "It's really about whether the membership wants me back and whether they just want me back. That’s what it’s about."
"I don't even think it’s Brian Rolapp or anybody like one of the top executives," he continued. "It's really if the players want me back and if not, then I understand that."
The Crushers GC captain didn't mention any specific names, while the PGA's Future Competition Committee of decision-makers features nine key players: Tiger Woods, Patrick Cantlay, Adam Scott, Camilo Villegas, Maverick McNealy, Keith Mitchell, Joe Gorder, John Henry, and Theo Epstein.
DeChambeau previously revealed he was "completely shocked" by the PIF’s reported decision to pull funding. He also noted that the PGA Tour 'isn’t doing great either' and indicated that its strong presence in mainstream and social media helps maintain a favorable public perception.
"They’ve got everybody on the side that helps pump it up," he added. "But they’re reducing field sizes, cutting employees, and restructuring their business too."
DeChambeau’s YouTube channel has exploded during his LIV era and now has 2.69 million subscribers, with 266 videos uploaded and more than 579,947,211 total views. His digital ambitions to scale up his content creation 'by three times or more' also pose a major threat to a PGA return.
PGA rules let players record personal content during tournaments, but they cannot livestream rounds or make money from on-site footage tied to the competition. DeChambeau admitted that the PGA didn't allow him to record, despite his repeated requests during his tenure from 2016 to 2022.
He declined the PGA Tour’s initial Returning Player program window earlier this year, with only Brooks Koepka accepting the pathway back under strict guidelines. Reports suggest that a second window opening could impose even greater sanctions on hopeful returning players.
